concepts.def: Phase when the Moon is between Earth and the Sun; the lit side faces away from Earth.
Right half of the Moon (Northern Hemisphere) is lit, one week after New Moon.
Earth is between Sun and Moon; the entire near side appears lit.
Left half of the Moon (Northern Hemisphere) is lit, three weeks after New Moon.
Time between successive same phases (e.g., New Moon to New Moon): 29.5 days.
Waxing = increasing lit fraction; waning = decreasing lit fraction.

walkthroughs.body_html:
The Lunar Disc — a core area of GCSE Astronomy.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Lunar Disc brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Lunar Disc.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

29.5 days
30.0 days
31.0 days

options: Full Moon
New Moon
First quarter
Gibbous

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse?
options: Lunar eclipses are more dangerous.
Straight lines that bend.
In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks the Sun; in a lunar eclipse Earth's shadow covers the Moon.
Solar eclipses happen by day, lunar at night - that is the only difference.

mcqs.q: Why don't we have a solar eclipse every new moon?
options: The Moon's orbit is tilted, so it usually passes above or below the Sun's apparent position.
Eclipses happen randomly.
Because clouds block them.
Lunar eclipses are more dangerous.
Because clouds block them.
Straight lines that bend.
Perfect circles.
Ellipses (Kepler's first law), with the Sun at one focus.
